title: OR Fire Safety & Airway Fire Protocol
keywords: the fire triangle in the OR is an oxidizer (supplemental oxygen or nitrous, often pooling under drapes), a fuel (drapes, prep solution, ETT, hair), and an ignition source (electrocautery, laser, fiber-optic light source)
the highest-risk combination is an open oxygen source near the head and neck during head/neck/upper-chest surgery with an ignition source nearby
airway fire — stop the gas flow, remove the burning tube, pour saline in the airway, then and only then reventilate with air before reintroducing oxygen
RACE for a general OR/hospital fire — Rescue, Alarm, Confine, Extinguish or Evacuate
let prep solution dry fully and avoid pooling before draping and before activating electrocautery
sources: American Society of Anesthesiologists. Practice Advisory for the Prevention and Management of Operating Room Fires. Anesthesiology. 2013;118(2):271-290.
ECRI Institute. New Clinical Guide to Surgical Fire Prevention.
Apfelbaum JL, et al. Practice Advisory for the Prevention and Management of Operating Room Fires: an updated report by the ASA Task Force.

changelog.change: Initial entry — a genuine content gap (Content audit 2026-09-15, fresh-look Batch 6). No prior module addressed OR fire prevention or the airway fire response, despite it being an ASA practice-advisory-mandated, safety-critical topic.

summary: OR fires happen when the fire triangle — oxidizer, fuel, ignition source — comes together, most dangerously during head/neck/upper-chest surgery with an open oxygen source; prevention is a team responsibility at every timeout, and an airway fire has a specific stop-remove-irrigate-reventilate sequence that has to be automatic.
whyThisMatters: Surgical fires are rare but devastating and largely preventable — nearly all of them involve the same recognizable combination of an oxygen-enriched atmosphere, a fuel source, and an ignition source close together, which is exactly why the ASA mandates an explicit fire-risk assessment at every surgical timeout. An airway fire specifically is a true emergency where the correct sequence (stop gas flow before anything else) has to be reflexive, not looked up in the moment.
clinicalTakeaway: Assess fire risk at every timeout — an open oxygen source near the head/neck plus an ignition source (electrocautery, laser) during head/neck/upper-chest surgery is the classic high-risk combination. Let prep solution dry fully and avoid pooling before draping/activating cautery. If a fire starts on the drapes/patient: RESCUE the patient, sound the ALARM, CONFINE by closing doors, and EXTINGUISH (or evacuate if it can't be controlled) — RACE. If an airway fire occurs: STOP the flow of airway gases immediately, REMOVE the burning endotracheal tube, POUR SALINE into the airway, THEN reventilate with air (mask ventilation) before reintroducing oxygen — do not reintroduce oxygen or reinsert an ETT until the fire is confirmed out.

body.text: The fire triangle in the OR

rows: Supplemental oxygen or nitrous oxide, especially an open source (nasal cannula, face mask, open delivery under drapes near the head) that can pool and create a locally oxygen-enriched atmosphere well above room air
Surgical drapes, prep solution (especially alcohol-based, if not fully dried), the endotracheal tube itself, patient hair, gauze/sponges
Electrocautery, laser, fiber-optic light source/cable (which can get hot enough to ignite drapes if left resting on them)

body.text: The highest-risk scenario is head/neck/upper-chest surgery with an open oxygen source near the surgical field AND an ignition source (electrocautery/laser) in use — this combination is exactly what the ASA fire-risk assessment at timeout is designed to catch.

items: Explicitly assess fire risk as part of the surgical timeout, especially for head/neck/upper-chest cases — this is an ASA practice-advisory expectation, not an optional extra step.
Allow alcohol-based or other flammable prep solutions to fully dry before draping, and avoid pooling of prep solution (especially in body folds/depressions) before activating any ignition source.

For open oxygen delivery near the face during head/neck surgery, coordinate with the surgeon to minimize supplemental oxygen concentration when electrocautery/laser is in active use near the field, if the patient's oxygenation allows it — an open, high-flow oxygen source right next to an active ignition source is the single most correctable risk factor.

Keep the fiber-optic light source cable off the drapes when not actively in the field, and use it only under direct attention — a light cable resting on drapes can generate enough heat to ignite them.

Communicate clearly between surgery, anesthesia, and nursing whenever an ignition source is about to be used near an oxygen-enriched field — this is a team safety moment, not any single role's sole responsibility.
RESCUE — remove the patient from the immediate fire source/area.
ALARM — activate the fire alarm/call for help per institutional protocol.
CONFINE — close doors to limit fire and smoke spread.
EXTINGUISH (if safe and the fire is small/controllable) or EVACUATE if it cannot be safely controlled.

body.text: Airway fire — the specific emergency sequence

An airway fire (during head/neck/upper-airway surgery, or from an ignition source near an oxygen-enriched airway) is a distinct emergency with its own sequence — this has to be automatic, not looked up in the moment.

items: 1. STOP the flow of airway gases immediately — disconnect the breathing circuit / stop all gas flow to the airway, including turning off supplemental oxygen and nitrous oxide.
2. REMOVE the burning material from the airway — this means removing the endotracheal tube (which may itself be burning or be the fuel source) if it's safe to do so.
3. POUR SALINE (or water) into the airway to extinguish any remaining fire.
4. Only AFTER the fire is confirmed extinguished: reventilate the patient with air (mask ventilation) — do NOT reintroduce oxygen or reinsert an endotracheal tube until the fire is out.

5. Once the patient is stabilized on air, reassess the airway (direct/bronchoscopic examination) for thermal injury before deciding how to proceed — reintubation, extent of injury, and ongoing management should be guided by what's actually found, not assumed.
6. Assess the patient for smoke inhalation injury and manage per standard inhalation-injury principles if significant airway/thermal injury is found.
